title: Trump confirms he switched planes after Nato summit because of possible threat
description: Figure caption, Watch: Trump tells reporters why he switched planesBySareen HabeshianUpdated 5 hours agoPresident Donald Trump has confirmed that he s
body: Figure caption, Watch: Trump tells reporters why he switched planesBySareen HabeshianUpdated 5 hours agoPresident Donald Trump has confirmed that he secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month due to a possible threat."I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane," Trump told reporters. "I just have to do what they say."The revelation comes after reports that Trump boarded Air Force One on 8 July in view of television cameras, before hiding in a catering truck to be transported to a military aircraft.The last-minute switch has raised questions about whether those left on the decoy plane were in danger, but Trump said on Tuesday the jet he boarded instead could have been at "greater risk... because that would be the plane, I think, that they would be more likely to go for."Officials told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the US had detected a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane. The New York Times reported that US intelligence had information of a person near the Nato summit who had been seen with a shoulder-fired missile.Journalists and some White House staff on board did not know the US president had been smuggled out as part of an elaborate ruse in response to a possible Iranian threat.Figure caption, Watch: Was Donald Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?Trump has previously said he was Iran's "number one target" during the summit in Ankara."I guess there was a threat out there," the president said during a visit aboard Air Force One to an event in Ohio on Tuesday. "I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats."He added: "I have a lot of threats that you don't know about."The clandestine manoeuvre last month came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran following a breakdown of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end the war.Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar, but announced that he would leave on the old Air Force One "for old time's sake".On 8 July, footage showed him boarding the presidential jet at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he slipped off Air Force One on to a catering truck that had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded.He was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president.Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the C-32A separately using external stairs in an effort to make the flight appear normal, according to the newspaper.Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board.A media pool producer who was on the plane said they found it unusual when they were told to keep the window shades down. A photographer briefly opened a shade and reportedly was quickly told to close it.The producer's comments were detailed in a report from the White House Correspondents' Association on Tuesday. They also noted there appeared to have been two catering trucks at both the front and back of the plane when the press arrived, and that the media van had been too far back in the motorcade at the airport be able to take a photo of the president boarding.Figure caption, Watch: Washington Post and AP reporters reveal details of plane swap over Iran threatTechnically "Air Force One" is the call sign for any aircraft carrying the US president. But on this occasion, the C-32A used the call sign "Reach 18", while the aircraft carrying the journalists continued to use "AF1" in order to keep up the ruse.Remaining on the original aircraft were members of Trump's cabinet, according to the New York Times. The outlet, citing two anonymous officials, reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were on board.Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet.The president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington.During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap.Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said at the time: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with."He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list".Jose Zamora, regional director for the Americas for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said in a statement that the Trump administration "has a responsibility to ensure that journalists covering the president are not unnecessarily exposed to danger"."Reporters should be informed of credible security threats so they can make informed decisions about their safety," he added.Figure caption, Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump?Additional reporting by Jessica Rawnsley

title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
description: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquak
body: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake. More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday.  While the official death toll remains at 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing. He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses. Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed. In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort. On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed. Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped.In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed.  The mayor of the municipality, Antonio Cadavid, stated that other children ended up with serious injuries, with a total of 30 children referred to care centres.To combat threats of looting, he has also ordered a curfew, coming into effect at 20:00 local time, and lasting until 06:00 on Wednesday morning. Hours after the earthquake hit Pereira, a resident of the Parque Industrial neighborhood, near the city's airport, told BBC Mundo about the shock being experienced in the area."It's impossible to get around the city center. In Bolívar Square (the city's main square), at least one building collapsed. Furthermore, there are structures where buses and trucks are trapped, and people are afraid those structures will collapse as well," he said."We're all in shock. It was really awful."Jorge Eduardo Rojas, mayor of Manizales, said five people had been killed in the city. Sixty buildings in Manizales had partially or totally collapsed. Cautioning about further aftershocks, Rojas urged the public not to share chain messages or social media posts from unknown sources, as they "may contain false or unverified information... which could cause greater concern and alarm among the public".  On Tuesday, help and support continued to be offered to Colombia from the international community. A statement from a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, stated that he "expresses his solidarity with the people and government of Colombia" and that it working to support the government's response.   Spain's Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, reported that 164 Spaniards were still missing.At the moment, he added, there are no reports of injuries or deaths of its citizens.The Trump administration, which backed President Abelardo de la Espriella in his successful election earlier this year, announced this afternoon a donation of $15.5m (£11.5m) to Colombia.Offers of help have also come from Ecuador, Brazil, El Salvador, and Venezuela.

title: Brother of man trapped under rubble in Colombian quake clings on to hope
description: Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building,
body: Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure."You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally.His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali.This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake.The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city.Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead.Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete.On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise."The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor.These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below.Velasco offers hope. "In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped.""Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds."I wanted to help from the very beginning."Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens."We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says.Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock."I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains.

title: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
description: On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey.But when the
body: On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey.But when the mighty Boeing aircraft left Ankara, the president had reportedly already been secretly spirited away via a catering truck to a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, which flew the president to RAF Mildenhall in the UK.Those left on board were unwitting decoys and had no indication that Trump was no longer travelling with them. But deception of this kind is not unusual."That's very common," said Ronald Kessler, an author who has written extensively on the agency. "There's a long history of strategies to mislead anybody who might be trying to harm the president."Robert McDonald, a former high-ranking Secret Service agent with experience working on presidential security details, told the BBC that smaller-scale deceptions are used frequently during motorcade operations.These motorcades - which often include dozens of security and support vehicles, as well as ambulances and vans carrying White House reporters - typically include two "Beasts", as the enhanced limousine carrying the president is known.While one vehicle carries the president, the other travels nearby as a decoy, switching locations while en route to the destination."It's what we call a shell game," said McDonald, who drove one of the vehicles during President George W Bush's administration. "Even in DC if we headed to Andrews [Joint Base Andrews - where Air Force One flies from], those two limousines would change position, like under a highway overpass." "But that would happen out of sight of anybody other than those in the motorcade or in that tunnel," he added. "Different things are used to mix up the bad guy."The exact nature of the perceived threat to the aircraft in this latest case remains unclear. The Secret Service has so far not commented on the incident, while the White House has neither confirmed nor denied it, saying only that it uses every tool available to protect the president.While contingency plans for a variety of scenarios are developed ahead of time, experts say that the Secret Service needs to maintain flexibility and remain poised to improvise in the face of new threats as they emerge, particularly overseas.But according to McDonald, the extraordinary measure of secretly moving President Trump from the aircraft suggests that the potential danger was deemed, likely by multiple agencies, to be serious."That tells me that the threat level in Turkey was relatively substantial and quite high," he said, adding that the president's staff, the Secret Service and the White House Military Office were almost certainly immediately alerted."Those people likely got together in a room and were presented with this intelligence," McDonald explained. "And a plan was put together to negate the threat from whatever intelligence was received."McDonald's assessment was echoed by Marc Polymeropoulos, a 26-year veteran of the CIA who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan and oversaw clandestine missions around the world."The key part of this is the nature of the threat, and what was so severe that the Secret Service would put forth such a deception operation," he said.A key question going forward, according to Polymeropoulos, is whether the government and intelligence community then had a duty to warn those on the aircraft."Let's say the plane was blown out of the sky, and we knew about it," he said. "We don't do that…we can't. If we know ISIS is going to attack a target in Moscow, we warn the Russians. Why do we warn the Russians? Because if there's an American citizen killed in that, we can't let that happen."How much danger those who remained on the aircraft were in - or whether they were in danger at all - remains unclear.Journalists on board reported that they were repeatedly instructed to keep their window blinds down, a "not uncommon" practice McDonald said shows that steps were still being taken to protect the passengers."A large plane flying overhead where somebody could see it, with the shades up and windows illuminated, could tell somebody that it's a particular type of aircraft," he said. "I appreciate the need for transparency, but [the passengers] are also part of the roadshow. We've got to make sure that you and everybody gets home safe."The Secret Service, he added, is under no legal obligation to inform of potential threats or detail operations being carried out to protect the president and his entourage. That decision would need to be made by the White House or other agencies."The Secret Service is not in the business of public relations," he said. "We're very good at keeping secrets, as our name says. Everybody doesn't need to know everything."

schema.headline: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight

title: Trump's secret plane swap highlights personal stakes of Iran war
description: "I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonatha
body: "I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonathan Karl, in a phone conversation the day after he launched the US military campaign against Iran in February.An Israeli airstrike, conducted with US approval and co-ordination, had just killed the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian leaders – and Trump drew a direct line from that attack to threats and alleged plots the Iranians had made against him in previous years.Trump has refrained from similar remarks in the ensuing six months of warfare, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed the view."Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh," he said in March, noting that an unnamed Iranian who he said led an assassination unit had been killed in US strikes.These comments hint at the personal nature of this war – and the concerns by the president and his security team of the threat Iran still poses to his safety.Those concerns were dramatically illustrated by this week's revelation that Trump secretly switched to an alternate aircraft on his flight back from the Nato summit in Turkey last month. He left the media and most of the White House staff to depart on the presidential Air Force One 747 jet, which became, essentially, a decoy.It was an elaborate ruse, which included the president being transported to and from aircraft inside a catering truck, in response to what American officials reportedly believed to be credible intelligence of an Iranian missile threat to Air Force One.The White House has given little detail about this threat - but nonetheless it marks another striking episode in the turbulent history of Trump's relationship with Iran.Government security experts have said such measures are not unusual when a president travels in or near a warzone. Past presidents have travelled to places like Afghanistan, Iraq and Ukraine under cover of secrecy – but never without at least some prior knowledge by media outlets, under agreements that they would not disclose the movement until after the fact.The optics of Trump hiding in a catering truck from an apparent Iranian threat are less than ideal for a president who has repeatedly touted his strength - as well as the frailty of Iran's military after months of war.The secrecy in the days and weeks after the Secret Service operation in Ankara may have been, in part, to avoid undermining his public image of power.The operation, which took more than a month to come to light, also underscores the apparent threat Iran continues to present to US interests in a conflict that the president asserts is all but wrapped up against an adversary he has said has been thoroughly defeated on the battlefield.Iranian threats against Trump are not new, however.After Trump, in his first term, ordered the January 2020 missile strike that killed Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) leader Qasem Soleimani, Iran's leaders promised reprisals against the American president and senior administration leaders.In one instance, an Iranian mural depicted a drone targeting Trump while he played golf in Florida.It appears that there were more to these Iranian threats than just posturing.The Biden administration warned Iran in 2022 not to target any US citizens, after unearthing a plan to target former Trump National Security Adviser John Bolton.And in July 2024, US law enforcement arrested a Pakistani man, Asif Merchant, who allegedly had ties to the IRGC, for plotting to kill Trump. Four months later, an Afghani citizen, Farhad Shakeri, was charged with another assassination scheme against Trump.Merchant was convicted in March 2026, but Shakeri, who US prosecutors allege was directed by an IRGC official, is still at large.Although these attempts were foiled during the planning stages, the physical risks Trump faced as he sought a return to the White House were all too apparent. In July 2024 he was left bloodied after a gunman opened fire at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. Two months later, an armed man was arrested in Florida after US Secret Service agents spotted him hiding in the trees near where Trump was playing golf."It was a galvanising moment for him," Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for the New York Times, said in a recent interview, external when discussing both the Iranian plots and assassination attempts of 2024. "All of that in his mind becomes one big blur.""For Trump himself, Iran and this feeling of being under threat is constant," she said.The president, according to the news website Semafor, external, often muses - and jokes - about becoming a target of assassination."Nobody told me how dangerous it is to be president, and if they had told me, I probably wouldn't have run," one White House official recounted Trump as saying. "And he makes comments like that in jest, but there's a reality behind that."Trump's bombing of Iran's nuclear research facilities in 2025, and this year's expansive bombing campaign and naval blockade, prompted a new round of Iranian threats against Trump – and a direct warning by the US president in response.In July, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had made threats "to assassinate, or attempt to assassinate" him and said 1,000 "missiles are Locked and Loaded and aimed at the Islamic Republic of Iran, with thousands more to immediately follow, should the Iranian Government act on its threat".The president's message to Iran was blunt. Many of the recent threats against him have been unequivocal, too.At the funeral service for Khamenei, held the day before Trump departed Turkey, participants carried a banner that read "#KillTrump". The following week, in a square in central Tehran, a building featured a large mural of the American president, lying in a black coffin, with the words "We will kill Trump" and "Blood for blood" written below it.Iran has denied involvement in any previous plots against Trump, but the message – delivered after Khamenei's death and reports of Iranian civilian casualties in US and Israeli strikes – has been clear.The war, Iranians are saying, is far from over. And Trump, himself, is a target for revenge.On the final leg of the journey back to the US from Turkey, as Trump and his travelling media pool were reunited on the same aircraft, the president came back to the press cabin to talk to reporters.They asked about the unusual journey, which included an order by the Secret Service that the window shades on the decoy plane be closed during takeoff from Ankara."I have read all the time I'm number one on their list," he told them. "But if I go, you go, right?"

schema.headline: Trump's secret plane swap highlights personal stakes of Iran war

title: Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump?
description: President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, according to US media. Footage from 8 July shows him boa
body: President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, according to US media. Footage from 8 July shows him boarding Air Force One, the presidential jet, at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president - via a catering truck, which had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded.Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board.The BBC's State Department correspondent Tom Bateman shares what it's like to be onboard Air Force One with the president as part of the press pool.Read more about the story here.

title: Assam: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar ByInd
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar ByIndia correspondentWell past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother.Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety."Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says.An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts.The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves.By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it.Image caption, Baruah quit journalism to concentrate on animal husbandryThe scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam.The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps.The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated.For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound."This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says.Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime.Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km.Image caption, A 97-year-old Lokada Duarah was carried onto a banana tree trunk and taken to safety after floodwaters rose around her homeImage source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, A boy uses a makeshift banana raft to navigate floodwaters in AssamShe had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building.Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'.Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it.She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed.None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says.The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly.Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages.About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp.Image caption, Baruah and her family abandoned their home nearly a day after the water began risingFor five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil.Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats.  Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill.But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before?Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley,  a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms".The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A family shelters inside a tent in Sivasagar district, among more than 5,000 people lodged in 252 relief campsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amit Giri holds a photo of his father, Siv Sankar Giri, who died in the floods, outside their damaged home in Sivasagar. He is among 100 people killed in the floods.As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251.In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat.Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology.Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam."What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography.For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal.Image caption, Only 60 of Baruah's goats survived the floodsShe has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week.Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have.So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life.She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance.Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee?"No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before.""We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."

schema.headline: Assam: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft

title: Singapore and South Korea pull Trader Joe's seasoning containing poppy seeds
description: Singapore and South Korea have pulled Trader Joe's Everything But the Bagel seasoning from e-commerce platforms because it contains poppy seeds.While
body: Singapore and South Korea have pulled Trader Joe's Everything But the Bagel seasoning from e-commerce platforms because it contains poppy seeds.While they do not naturally contain opiates, poppy seeds are banned in both countries because they can get contaminated with opiates by fluid in the poppy plant during harvesting.More than 20 online listings of the popular seasoning have been removed, Singapore's Central Narcotics Bureau said on Wednesday.Last week, Seoul authorities said the seasoning tested positive for morphine and codeine, which are opiates found in the plant's sap.Apart from poppy seeds, the product also contains sesame seeds, sea salt, minced garlic and minced onion. It was released by American grocery chain Trader Joe's in 2017.Authorities in Singapore have urged anyone who has bottles of the seasoning to dispose of them."Singapore adopts a strict policy of zero tolerance towards controlled drugs," the narcotics bureau said, according to a CNA report."The possession, consumption, importation, exportation, manufacturing and trafficking of any controlled drug, even in trace amounts, is an offence under the Misuse of Drugs Act," it said.In South Korea, investigators say some people brought the seasoning back home as souvenirs from their overseas trips before listing it for resale.Some did so without realising it contained controlled substances, while others did so knowingly, according to a report by The Korea Herald."Even if a product is legally sold overseas, it may be classified as a narcotic substance or a prohibited import in Korea, so particular caution is required," a police official said.

title: New Zealand PM survives second leadership challenge ahead of election
description: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a vote of confidence before a general election due in November, saying he has the "full supp
body: New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a vote of confidence before a general election due in November, saying he has the "full support" of his ruling National Party.Luxon had called for an "urgent" meeting with his National Party caucus on Wednesday to address "‌increased speculation about [his] leadership"."I have the full support of our caucus... Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he told reporters after the meeting which lasted more than three hours.This was the second challenge to his leadership in four months. Support for Luxon and his party remained weak amid sluggish economic growth and a series of missteps by the leader.Last week, Luxon drew backlash after suggesting a possible referendum on the country's electoral system on live radio, without prior consultation with his party colleagues.Earlier this month, the 56-year-old riled up New Zealand's business community after a speech calling on small business owners to "be adult". He said the country's businesses had a "parent-child mentality" with the central government and relied too often on handouts.He later apologised and acknowledged many were going through tough times.The former Air New Zealand boss led his centre-right party to victory in the 2023 elections vowing to bring down the cost of living and reduce taxes."My pledge to you is that our government will deliver for every New Zealander," he said then.But his party has suffered in opinion polls in recent months as the economy continues to stall, with unemployment rising to an 11-year high of 5.6%.A 1News Verian poll published on Wednesday morning showed Luxon's preferred prime minister rating slide to 17% – a new low for his time in office – but he remains ahead of all other candidates included in the poll.New Zealand will hold its next general election on 7 November.

schema.headline: New Zealand PM survives second leadership challenge ahead of election

body: Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated by tropical storms, was equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas. It resulted in school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the capital. Floods, landslides and accidents driven by the rains killed at least 16 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said on Monday

title: Watch: Why was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?

body: Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported.The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US.Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane. The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams explains.More on this story: Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say

title: Tata Group Chairman N Chandrasekaran to step down in February
description: N Chandrasekaran, the chairman of Tata Group, has said that he will not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.The 63-year-old said the dec
body: N Chandrasekaran, the chairman of Tata Group, has said that he will not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.The 63-year-old said the decision came after the board of Tata Sons could not reach a resolution on a five-year extension of his term, months after the proposal first came up.The news sent shares of listed Tata companies plunging and has led to questions over what lies ahead for the gigantic salt-to-steel conglomerate that owns Air India, Tata Steel and Jaguar Land Rover.Chandrasekaran's resignation, which comes days ahead of Tata Sons' annual general meeting, points to tensions that have been playing out for months after a boardroom power battle erupted between trustees.The Tata Group is uniquely structured - a charitable arm called Tata Trusts owns 66% of the group's parent company, Tata Sons. This has given the group tax and regulatory advantages, and allows it to carry out charitable activities, but experts say that its dual non-profit and commercial objectives have sometimes led to governance issues.Tata Trusts has three nominees on the Tata Sons board. Reports have said that the board members have disagreed over issues such as board nominations, funding approvals and the public listing of Tata Sons. The group has not publicly commented on the discord.Tata Group - the divided empire facing boardroom dramaThe internal rifts threatened to distract the group while it was facing severe business headwinds including the revival of Air India, which it bought from the Indian government in 2022.When the proposal for his extension was brought before the board in February, one board member did not support it, Chandrasekaran said in his statement without naming the person."In the absence of unanimous support, I chose to defer the decision," he said, adding that there was no resolution even six months later."Tata Sons is a very large institution and there are many strategic projects that are under critical stages of execution. It is not only necessary to have a leader in place to lead the Group beyond Feb 2027, but also clarity on leadership is important for employees, investors, partners and other stakeholders," he said.Chandrasekaran was named the group's chairman in 2017. He replaced the late Cyrus Mistry, whose abrupt removal from the post months earlier had triggered a bitter legal battle.

title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
description: Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital pu
body: Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment.A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it.The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure.Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row.Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced.Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity.The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law."We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC.As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon."We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said.Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004.Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security.Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008.Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East.Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017.In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed.Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023.Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent".In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said earlier this month.

schema.headline: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
